newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH LEGISLATORS RACE TO PASS NEW CONSTITUTION.
newsitem.headline: POLISH LEGISLATORS RACE TO PASS NEW CONSTITUTION.

text.p: Poland's national assembly of both houses of parliament on Monday began a week's debate on the draft of a new constitution which has become an ideological battleground in the approach to general elections.

Years after the 1989 fall of communism made Poland's 1952 constitution obsolete, the ruling leftist coalition and the main opposition parties in parliament have agreed principles of a compromise draft, facing its second reading this week.

They hope to pass and submit it to a referendum before elections due in September, which are likely to return to parliament rightist, pro-Catholic Church parties largely absent from the current legislature dominated by ex-communists.

These parties, mostly grouped around the Solidarity trade union support their own draft, in which the Christian idea of natural law takes precedence over codified laws, and would seek to profoundly re-work parliament's current proposal if they win the polls before the constitution is passed.

Poland's ex-communist president Aleksander Kwasniewski recognised on Monday that parliament's version was not ideal, but strongly supported the document thrashed out by the four major parliamentary parties after three years' work.

"The dilemma we face together is do we want to wait for an ideal constitution -- which we don't have -- or support this good one which will organise public and social life and the law in Poland for many years," he told a news conference.

Criticising Solidarity's so-called Citizens' Draft, Kwasniewski said: "The principle that natural law takes precedence over codified law...cannot appear in any constitution of a state which is secular or neutral in its world view."

The head of the biggest rightist opposition grouping, Marian Krzaklewski of Solidarity Election Action (AWS) has agreed to join the national assembly debate this week, to argue for the adoption of key tenets of the Citizens' Draft.
These include an anti-abortion provision guaranteeing protection of life right right from conception, and guarantees of social security provisions to safeguard families.
Solidarity chief Krzaklewski is unlikely to secure major concessions on such issues and he said last week that he would not contemplate "rotten compromises".
The other major rightist party, the Movement for the Reconstruction of Poland (ROP), has refused even to talk of a possible compromise.

"I think it is better to wait for a while than to pass a constitution which from the very outset will be contested and questioned by the majority of public opinion," Jan Olszewski, head of the rightist Movement for the Reconstruction of Poland, told public radio on Monday.

The Citizen's Draft attracted many hundreds of thousands of signatures of support in largely Catholic Poland when it was submitted two years ago and opinion polls suggest it has wide backing, as do its sponsors.

A February poll by the public CBOS institute, published last week, showed the Solidarity alliance with 24 percent support, ahead of the ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) with 22 percent.
Solidarity has been demanding that the referendum should allow the public to choose between the two drafts -- a proposal rejected by the ruling parties.
